claims.text: Lightweight high-entropy alloys are low-density metallic structural materials with high strength-to-weight ratios.
High mixing entropy stabilizes a predominantly disordered solid-solution microstructure.
A disordered solid solution with minimal elemental segregation suppresses deleterious intermetallic phases.
Increasing copper content in AlCrTiV0.5Cux alloys promotes copper segregation.
Increasing copper content induces precipitate formation.
Copper-induced segregation causes the combined strength, ductility, corrosion-resistance, and oxidation-resistance synergy to be lost.
Low-copper AlCrTiV0.5 has a single-phase, disordered microstructure with uniformly distributed elements.
Above a critical copper concentration, significant phase separation and secondary-phase precipitation occur.
High mixing entropy produces a metastable single-phase structure that minimizes nucleation sites for deleterious precipitates.
Maintaining a uniform atomic environment prevents localized corrosion.
Maintaining a uniform atomic environment prevents early oxidation.
Maintaining a uniform atomic environment refines the microstructure and thereby enhances mechanical strength.
Higher-copper alloys will exhibit higher corrosion current densities than the low-copper baseline.
Higher-copper alloys will exhibit increased oxidation degradation rates relative to the baseline.
Higher-copper alloys will exhibit lower mechanical strength relative to the baseline.
Higher-copper alloys will exhibit lower ductility relative to the baseline.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis explicitly predicts that copper-induced segregation causes property degradation, but the conditions and boundary fields describe segregation as the point at which the hypothesis itself ceases to hold. Segregation is therefore presented both as a tested causal regime of the hypothesis and as outside its applicability.
